overview: Both describe evolutionary change, differing mainly in scale and timeframe — small shifts within a species versus the origin of new species or higher groups.
genZNote: Microevolution: small tweaks within a generation or few. Macroevolution: the big picture, zoomed way out over deep time.

aspects.label: Scale of Change
aspects.valueA: Small-scale changes in allele frequency within a single population or species.
aspects.valueB: Large-scale evolutionary change, often resulting in new species or higher taxonomic groups.

aspects.label: Typical Timeframe
aspects.valueA: Can be observed over a few generations.
aspects.valueB: Occurs over very long geological timescales, often studied through the fossil record.

aspects.label: Example
aspects.valueA: Antibiotic resistance evolving in a bacterial population.
aspects.valueB: The evolution of birds from theropod dinosaurs.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: Macroevolution is essentially the accumulated result of many microevolutionary changes over vast timescales, not a fundamentally different mechanism.
overlay.memoryTrick: Micro = small changes, short term. Macro = big changes, long term.
overlay.commonMisconception: Macroevolution is not a separate, mysterious process from microevolution — most biologists view it as the long-term outcome of the same processes (selection, drift, mutation) accumulating over time.
